title: Unknown persistence can be recovered from four autocovariances up to economic labels
scope: Population identification of the source's two independent stationary Gaussian AR(1) components when both persistence coefficients are unknown and distinct.
significance: Derives explicit Prony-type recovery from lags zero through three and proves the remaining label-switching ambiguity, separating statistical component recovery from naming the neutral rate.
body:
# Unknown persistence recovery up to component labels

The source identifies component variances when distinct persistence parameters are known. In its independent stationary Gaussian model, four population autocovariances also recover the unknown persistence parameters, but only up to exchanging the economic labels. That distinction matters for identifying a “neutral” component.

Write \(U=V_q>0\), \(V=\sigma^2V_d>0\), and assume unknown distinct \(\alpha,\beta\in(-1,1)\). The observable centered covariance sequence is
\[
\Gamma_j=U\alpha^j+V\beta^j,\qquad j\ge0.
\]
Define
\[
D=\Gamma_0\Gamma_2-\Gamma_1^2.
\]
Direct expansion gives
\[
D=UV(\alpha-\beta)^2>0.
\tag{A}
\]
Thus distinct persistence and two nondegenerate independent components leave a specific observable rank signature.

Let \(S=\alpha+\beta\), \(P=\alpha\beta\). Each exponential obeys the same second-order recurrence, hence
\[
\Gamma_{j+2}=S\Gamma_{j+1}-P\Gamma_j.
\]
Using \(j=0,1\) and solving the two linear equations yields
\[
S=\frac{\Gamma_0\Gamma_3-\Gamma_1\Gamma_2}{D},
\qquad
P=\frac{\Gamma_1\Gamma_3-\Gamma_2^2}{D}.
\tag{B}
\]
The two persistence coefficients are the distinct real roots of
\(z^2-Sz+P=0\). Once an ordering is selected, their associated variances are
\[
U=\frac{\Gamma_1-\beta\Gamma_0}{\alpha-\beta},
\qquad
V=\frac{\alpha\Gamma_0-\Gamma_1}{\alpha-\beta}.
\tag{C}
\]
These formulas recover all four covariance parameters from lags zero through three.

For necessity, (A) and the recurrence establish every equation. For sufficiency within the declared two-component class, any other parameter quadruple reproducing those four autocovariances must have the same \(S,P\), hence the same two roots. Equations (C) then determine the associated weights uniquely. Consequently the only remaining covariance-parameter ambiguity is their simultaneous exchange. All later covariance values are fixed by the recurrence; in the centered Gaussian class this determines the whole observable law.

The economic label ambiguity is real. Exchanging \((\alpha,U)\) and \((\beta,V)\) preserves every observed covariance. With known \(\sigma>0\), assign the new \(q\) stationary variance \(V\) and the new demand component stationary variance \(U/\sigma^2\). Their independent innovations remain admissible. Nothing in the observed residual says which recovered persistence belongs to the neutral rate. An economically defended ordering restriction, external measurement or another exclusion is needed to attach that name to a root.

For illustration, \(\alpha=1/5,\beta=4/5,U=V=1\) produces
\[
(\Gamma_0,\Gamma_1,\Gamma_2,\Gamma_3)
=(2,1,17/25,13/25).
\]
Then \(D=9/25\), (B) gives \(S=1,P=4/25\), and the roots are exactly \(1/5,4/5\). Both economic labelings fit equally well.

If \(D=0\), the distinct-positive-components class is rejected. Equal persistence, a vanishing variance or a misspecified component model must be considered instead. Formula (A) also shows why near-coincident roots or nearly absent components make recovery unstable: the denominators in (B) shrink. Population recovery does not imply informative finite-sample estimates.

This result does not recover unknown component means, reveal realized latent states, or identify the flexible-price long-run rate. Those remain separate obstructions in the source. It adds unknown-transition parameter recovery only under its strong independence, stationarity, Gaussianity and two-component restrictions, without an empirical neutral-rate estimate.

title: Sharp eventual-selection bounds when commitment speeds are heterogeneous
scope: Extension of the source's empirical-profile timing model to an arbitrary distribution of positive commitment hazards within one equilibrium-destined group.
significance: Shows two-horizon homogeneous inversion identifies the minimum possible eventual mass and derives the complete sharp eventual-selection interval under speed heterogeneity.
body:
# Eventual-selection bounds under heterogeneous commitment speed

The source's two-horizon inversion is exact for one geometric commitment hazard per equilibrium. If hazards vary across groups destined for the same equilibrium, the same observations generally identify only a lower bound on eventual selection. The complete identified interval can still be computed.

Keep the source's empirical-profile neighborhoods and off-diagonal precommitment path. Fix one equilibrium, let \(w\in[0,1]\) be its eventual group mass, and draw its commitment hazard \(\rho\in(0,1]\) from an arbitrary distribution. Conditional on that hazard, waiting time remains geometric as in the source. The remaining groups do not enter this equilibrium's neighborhood. Its probabilities at horizons four and eight are
\[
u=q(4)=wE[\rho],\qquad
v=q(8)=wE[2\rho-\rho^2].
\tag{A}
\]
Every positive hazard eventually commits almost surely, so \(w\) is indeed the eventual mass, even without a uniform positive lower hazard bound.

If \(u>0\) and \(u<v\), the data are compatible exactly when
\[
v\le2u-u^2,
\]
and the sharp identified interval is
\[
w\in\left[\frac{u^2}{2u-v},\,1\right].
\tag{B}
\]
For \(v=u>0\), instead \(w=u\) and the hazard equals one almost surely. If \(u=0\), positive hazards imply \(w=0\) and therefore \(v=0\). Values outside these cases reject the subclass.

For necessity in the nondegenerate case, (A) gives
\[
E[\rho]=u/w,\qquad E[\rho^2]=(2u-v)/w.
\]
Nonnegative variance implies \(u^2\le w(2u-v)\), yielding the lower bound in (B). Since \(w\le1\), it also implies the stated compatibility inequality. The strict inequality \(v<2u\) follows automatically from \(E[\rho^2]>0\). Moreover \(\rho^2\le\rho\) gives \(v\ge u\). Equality requires \(\rho\in\{0,1\}\) almost surely; positivity excludes zero, proving the separate \(v=u\) conclusion.

For sharpness, take any \(w\) in (B) and put \(m=u/w\), \(s=(2u-v)/w\). They satisfy \(0<m<1\), \(m^2\le s<m\). The two-point hazard distribution supported on
\[
\ell=\frac{m-s}{1-m}\in(0,m],\qquad 1
\]
has the required moments when the probability on one is
\[
\pi=\frac{m-\ell}{1-\ell}.
\]
Indeed \(E\rho=m\), and \(E\rho^2=m(1+\ell)-\ell=s\). At \(s=m^2\), \(\ell=m,\pi=0\), giving a constant hazard. All hazards are strictly positive and at most one. Give mass \(w\) this timing law and let the remainder stay off diagonal forever. The construction reproduces both observations and attains every eventual mass in (B).

For \(u=0.2,v=0.3\), the exact interval is \(w\in[0.4,1]\). The source's homogeneous inversion gives hazard \(0.5\) and mass \(0.4\), the lower endpoint. The same finite-horizon data also fit eventual mass one: choose hazard \(1/8\) with probability \(32/35\) and hazard one with probability \(3/35\). These give \(E\rho=1/5\) and \(E\rho^2=1/10\), hence exactly the observed probabilities.

Other equilibria can impose a further common mass constraint; (B) treats this one equilibrium with all remaining groups permitted to remain unclassified. Allowing zero hazards would change the interpretation of a “destined” mass and the equality boundary.

The source makes its homogeneous-hazard restriction explicit, so this is a partial-identification extension, not an error claim. It does not identify unknown learning rules, validate belief-report kernels or establish portability across games.

title: Global optimality with positive recruitment costs requires an exact operating-profit bound
scope: Constant-elasticity recruitment/separation construction with a known positive recruit resource cost and an explicit zero-profit nonoperation option.
significance: Extends the source's sharp construction beyond zero recruitment cost and proves the necessary/sufficient global operating condition, preserving full optimization rather than relying on a first-order condition.
body:
# Global optimality with positive recruitment costs

The source correctly restricts its sharp global construction to zero recruitment resource cost. With positive cost, its flow-corrected first-order identity remains necessary but needs an operating-profit condition. In the same constant-elasticity family, that condition is exact and sufficient for a global optimum.

Fix observed \(w_0,n_0,s_0>0\), separation elasticity \(b>0\), recruitment elasticity \(a\ge0\), and cost per recruit \(h\ge0\). Define
\[
R(w)=s_0n_0(w/w_0)^a,\qquad
s(w)=s_0(w/w_0)^{-b},\qquad e=a+b.
\]
Employment is \(n(w)=n_0(w/w_0)^e\). Choose productivity according to the source's corrected identity:
\[
m=w_0(1+1/e)+hs_0a/e.
\tag{A}
\]
Then \(w_0\) is stationary for steady-state profit
\(\Pi(w)=(m-w)n(w)-hR(w)\).

The exact condition for \(w_0\) to be a global maximizing operating wage, weakly preferred to not operating, is
\[
hs_0b\le w_0.
\tag{B}
\]
At strict inequality it strictly beats nonoperation and is the unique overall optimum. At equality it is the unique positive operating-wage maximizer but ties the zero-profit nonoperation option.

Necessity follows by evaluating profit at \(w_0\). Substitution of (A) gives
\[
\Pi(w_0)=\frac{n_0}{e}(w_0-hs_0b).
\tag{C}
\]
A negative value cannot maximize when not operating yields zero.

For sufficiency, first take \(a>0\) and \(h>0\). The sign of \(\Pi'(w)\) is the sign of
\[
F(w)=em-(e+1)w-hs_0a(w/w_0)^{-b}.
\]
It is strictly concave on positive wages, tends to minus infinity at both ends, and vanishes at \(w_0\). Its derivative there is
\[
F'(w_0)=-(e+1)+hs_0ab/w_0.
\]
Under (B), \(F'(w_0)\le-(e+1)+a=-(b+1)<0\). Therefore \(w_0\) is the larger root. There is exactly one smaller root: strict concavity, the negative endpoint limits and the negative derivative at \(w_0\) imply that \(F\) is positive just below \(w_0\) and crosses zero once before that. Profit decreases, then increases, then decreases across these two roots. Its only candidate global maximum is consequently \(w_0\) or the limiting value at zero. That limit is zero, approached from below because the negative recruitment term has exponent \(a<e\). Equation (C) makes \(w_0\) at least as good, proving sufficiency and uniqueness among positive wages.

If \(h=0\), the source's direct unimodality proof applies. If \(a=0\), recruitment expenditure is constant and profit's variable part is proportional to \((m-w)w^b\), uniquely maximized at \(w_0\); condition (C) again handles nonoperation. Thus all declared corners are covered.

This also sharpens partial identification with known \(h\). If recruitment elasticity lies in a supplied interval and (B) holds, every \(a\) in that interval generates a globally optimal observed wage with productivity (A). Its derivative is
\[
\frac{dm}{da}=\frac{hs_0b-w_0}{(a+b)^2}\le0.
\]
At the participation boundary, inferred productivity is constant across recruitment elasticities; below it, higher recruitment elasticity lowers the required productivity. If (B) fails, no member of this stationary family can explain an operating global optimum at \(w_0\).

The conclusion remains about steady-state partial-equilibrium profit. It does not solve a discounted workforce control problem, identify recruitment costs from quits, or include competitor reactions. It extends the source's constructive optimization guarantee while respecting those limits.
